## Q2 (Conditional expectation)

### 1. Deriving the conditional distribution of y given x.

$$\begin{align*}
  &f_{Y|X}(y|x=\hat{x}) = \frac{f_{Y,X}(y,x=\hat{x})}{f_X(x=\hat{x})} && \text{b.d.} \\
  &= \frac{\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_y\sigma_x(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}
      \left[\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)^2-2\rho\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)+\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)^2
      \right] \right\}}
    {\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_x}
      \text{exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2}
        \left[\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}
        \right]^2
    \right)} && \text{b.d.} \\
  &= \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_x}{2\pi\sigma_y\sigma_x(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{
      -\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}
      \left[\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)^2-2\rho\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)+\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)^2
      \right] 
+
      \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right]^2 * \frac{1-\rho^2}{1-\rho^2}
    \right\} \\
  &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_y(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\left[
      \left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)^2-2\rho\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)+\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)^2 
-
      \left[\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right]^2 + \rho^2 \left[\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right]^2
    \right]\right\} \\
  &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_y(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\left[
      \left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)^2-2\rho\left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right)\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right) + \rho^2 \left[\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right]^2
    \right]*\frac{\sigma_y^2}{\sigma_y^2}\right\}
\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}
f_{Y|X}(y|x=\hat{x}) 
  &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_y(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_y^2(1-\rho^2)}
      \left[
      \left(\frac{y-\mu_y}{\sigma_y}\right) -
      \rho\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)
      \right]^2*\sigma_y^2\right\} \\
  &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_y(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_y^2(1-\rho^2)}
      \left[
      y-\mu_y -
      \sigma_y\rho\left(\frac{x-\mu_x}{\sigma_x}\right)
      \right]^2\right\} \\
  &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_y(1-\rho^2)^\frac{1}{2}} 
    \text{exp}\left\{-\frac{1}{2\sigma_y^2(1-\rho^2)}
      \left[
      y-\mu_y -
      \rho\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}(x-\mu_x)
      \right]^2\right\} \\
  \therefore y | x &\sim N\left(\mu_y + \rho\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}(x-\mu_x), \sigma_y^2(1-\rho^2)\right) && \text{b.c.} \\
\end{align*}$$

As desired, we get the equation from slide 121 of "Conditional Expectations"! This suggests that the distribution of y given x is normal, with the mean and deviation listed above.

### 2. Compute the linear projection of $y$ on $\vec{x} = (1,x)$; that is, express $L(y|1,x)$ as a function of $\mu_x,\mu_y,\rho,\sigma_x,\sigma_y$.

Let's assume—based on the dimensionality of the objects at play—that $L(y|\vec{x}) = \vec{x}'\beta$, where $\beta = (\beta_0, \beta_1)$. We can then solve for the elements of beta individually, based on the equations in Note 1. More specifically, we use the simplified forms for the case in which $\text{dim}(\bar{\beta})=1$ .

$$\begin{align*}
  \beta_0 &= E[y]-E[x]\beta_1 && \text{see (7), Notes 1} \\
  \bar{\beta} &= [Var(\bar{x})]^{-1}Cov(\bar{x},y) && \text{see (10), Notes 1} \\
  \implies \beta_1 &= cov(x,y)/var(x) && \text{b.c. dim}(\bar{\beta}) = 1
\end{align*}$$

Because $\beta_0$'s equation includes $\beta_1$, we solve for the latter first.

$$\begin{align*}
  \beta_1 &= cov(x,y)/var(x) \\
  &= \frac{\sigma_x\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x^2} && \text{from the covariance matrix} \\
  &= \frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x}
\end{align*}$$

Plugging that in, we get $\beta_0 = E[y]-E[x]\beta_1 = \mu_y - \mu_x\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x}$.

Per the definition of linear projection, this means that

$$\begin{align*}
L(y|\vec{x}) &= \vec{x}'\beta \\
  &= \beta_0 + x\beta_1 \\
  &= \mu_y-\mu_x\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x} + x\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x} \\
  &= \mu_y+\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x}(x-\mu_x)
\end{align*}$$

Interestingly, this matches the mean of y\|x (from part 1)!

### 3. Define $u=y-L(y|1,x)$. What is the distribution of $u$?

$$\begin{align*}
u &= y - L(y|\vec{x}) \\
  &= y - (\mu_y+\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x}(x-\mu_x)) \\
  &= (y-\mu_y)-\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x}(x-\mu_x)\\
\end{align*}$$

Since $u$, here, is a linear combination of jointly normal variables, we assume that u too must be normally distributed. Equation (5) in Notes 01 tells us that the mean of $u$ is 0 (since the first element of $\bar{x}$ is 1), so all that's left to determine is the variance. Per Slide 32 of the probability review...

$$\begin{align*}
Var(u) &= (-\frac{\sigma_y\rho}{\sigma_x})^2Var(x) + Var(y) \\
  &= \frac{\sigma_y^2\rho^2}{\sigma_x^2}\sigma_x^2+\sigma_y^2 \\
  &= \sigma_y^2\rho^2+\sigma_y^2 \\
  &= \sigma_y^2(1+\rho^2) \\
  & \implies u \sim N(0, \sigma_y^2(1+\rho^2))
\end{align*} \\$$

## Q3 (Linear projection)

Looks like I was using the Notes 01's re-derivation of these equations, whoops! Anyway, to re-derive them (as suggested, reverse-engineering Notes 01): Define $\pmb{x}= (x_1, ..., x_K)$ as a 1 × K vector, and make the assumption that the K × K variance matrix of x is nonsingular (positive definite). Then the linear projection of $y$ on $1,x_1,x_2,\dots,x_K$ always exists and is unique: $L(y|1,x_1,\dots,x_K)=L(y|1,\pmb{x})=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\dots+B_Kx_K=\beta_0+\pmb{x}\beta$.

Proceeding from the definitions of $\beta_0$ and $\beta$ under linear projection...

$$\begin{align*}
\beta_0 &= E[y]-E[\pmb{x}]\beta \\
\beta &= [Var(\pmb{x})]^{-1}Cov(\pmb{x},y)\\
\implies Var(\pmb{x})\beta &= Cov(\pmb{x},y) && \text{left-multiplying by Var}(\pmb{x})\\
[E[\pmb{x}'\pmb{x}]-E[\pmb{x}']E[\pmb{x}]]\beta&=E[\pmb{x}'y] - E[\pmb{x}']E[y] && \text{(1) b.d. of Var(), Cov()} \\
&\text{Pulling down the first equation...} \\
\beta_0 &= E[y]-E[\pmb{x}]\beta \\
\beta_0 + E[\pmb{x}]\beta &= E[y] && (2)\\
E[\pmb{x}']\beta_0 + E[\pmb{x}']E[\pmb{x}]\beta &= E[\pmb{x}']E[y] && \text{(3) left-multiplying by}E[\pmb{x}']\\
E[\pmb{x}']\beta_0+E[\pmb{x}'\pmb{x}]\beta&=E[\pmb{x}'y] &&\text{(4) adding (1) and (3)} \\
\begin{pmatrix}1&E[\pmb{x}]\\E[\pmb{x}']&E[\pmb{x}'\pmb{x}]\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta\end{pmatrix} &= \begin{pmatrix}E[y]\\E[\pmb{x}'y]\end{pmatrix} &&\text{(5) combining (2) and (4)} \\
\end{align*}$$

Define $\bar{x}=(1,x_1,\dots,x_K)=(1,\pmb{x})$ and $\bar{\beta}=(\beta_0,\beta_1,\dots,\beta_K)=(\beta_0,\beta)$. Then

$$\begin{align*}
\begin{pmatrix}1&E[\pmb{x}]\\E[\pmb{x}']&E[\pmb{x}'\pmb{x}]\end{pmatrix} = E[\bar{x}'\bar{x}]&, \begin{pmatrix}E[y]\\E[\pmb{x}'y]\end{pmatrix}=E[\bar{x}'y]
 && \text{by the definition of }\bar{x}\\
E[\bar{x}'\bar{x}]\bar{\beta} &= E[\bar{x}'y] && \text{modified from (5)}\\
\end{align*}$$

With $L(y|\bar{x})=\bar{x}\bar{\beta}$, we now have a definition (and equations for) the linear projection equivalent to Notes 01 (with swapped notation).

Intuitively, the only difference between these two definitions is a re-parameterization; otherwise, they're identical, as seen above!

## Q4 (Asymptotics, asymptotic normality)

### 1. Let $\bar{y}_N$ denote the sample average based on a sample size of N. Find $Var\left(\sqrt{N}(\bar{y}_N-\mu)\right)$.

$$\begin{align*}
Var\left(\sqrt{N}(\bar{y}_N-\mu)\right) &= Var\left(\sqrt{N}\bar{y}_N\right) \\
&= NVar\left(\bar{y}_N\right) \\
&= NVar\left( \frac{1}{N} \sum^{N}_{i=1} y_i \right) \\
&= \frac{N}{N^2}Var\left(\sum^{N}_{i=1} y_i \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{i=1} Var\left(y_i \right)  && \text{bc iid}\\
&= \frac{1}{N}\sum^{N}_{i=1} \sigma^2 \\
&= \sigma^2 \\
\end{align*}$$

### 2. What is the asymptotic variance of $\sqrt{N}(\bar{y}_N-\mu)$?

Since $Var\left(\sqrt{N}(\bar{y}_N-\mu)\right)$ does not depend on N, $$\lim_{N\to\infty} Var\left(\sqrt{N}(\bar{y}_N-\mu)\right) = \sigma^2 \\$$

### 3. What is the asymptotic variance of $\bar{y}_N$ ? Compare this with $Var(\bar{y}_N)$?

$$\begin{align*}
Var(\bar{y}_N) &= Var\left( \frac{1}{N} \sum^{N}_{i=1} y_i \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{N^2} Var\left( \sum^{N}_{i=1} y_i \right) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum^{N}_{i=1} Var\left(y_i \right)  && \text{bc iid}\\
&= \frac{1}{N^2}\sum^{N}_{i=1} \sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{N} && Var(\bar{y}_N)\\
\lim_{N\to\infty} Var(\bar{y}_N) &= 0 && \text{asymptotic variance}\\
\end{align*}$$

Unlike questions (1) and (2), we see genuine convergence here! More specifically, while $Var(\bar{y}_N)$ is non-zero, it converges towards zero as $N\to\infty$.

### 4. What is the asymptotic standard deviation of $\bar{y}_N$

Since the standard deviation is the square root of variance, the answer here—like above—is 0!

## Q5 (Simulation and Asymptotics)

### 1. What is $Var(y_i)$?

$$\begin{align*}
Var(y_i) &= Var(1+x_i+\varepsilon_i) \\
 &= Var(1) + Var(x_i) + Var(\varepsilon_i) \\
 &= 0 + 4 + 40 \\
Var(y_i) &= 44 \\
\end{align*}$$

### 2. Using the derivation from Q4, calculate the value of the asymptotic variance of $\bar{y}_N$ where $N=100$.

I'm a little confused about the wording of this question, which I'm worried may reflect an improperly completed question 4. However, confirming my answers with the "Asymptotic Theory II" slides, I'm going to assume the question here is meant to read "what's the variance when N=100" (since the asymptotic variance converges to 0).

$$\begin{align*}
\bar{y}_{100} &= \frac{\sigma^2}{N} \\
&= \frac{44}{100} \\
&= 0.44 \\
\end{align*}$$

### 3. Now, using Monte Carlo simulation as in the lab session note, calculate $Var(\bar{y}_N)$. Confirm that this number is similar to what you obtained from 2.

```{r}
rm(list = ls()); # refresh memory

my_random_seed = 42; # seed for the random number generator
set.seed(my_random_seed); # setting the seed of the random number generator

generate_data = function(N = 100){
  # simulating data
  mat_data = matrix(NA, N, 2); # N by 2 matrix to store (y,x) by row
  for (i in 1:N){
    e = rchisq(1, df=20) - 20
    x = rnorm(1, mean=1, sd = sqrt(4)); # x~N(1,4)
    y = 1 + x + e; # this is our population model
    mat_data[i,] = c(y,x);
  }
  colnames(mat_data) = c("y", "x"); # put column names
  return(mat_data);
}

simulation_sample_mean = function(N=100, M=1000){
  # A function that generates M data sets (length of N), computes sample mean of each data set
  # N: the length of each data set
  # M: the number of simulations (that is, the number of data sets)
  mat_theta_hat = matrix(NA, M, 1); # a placeholder to collect M sample means
  for (m in 1:M){
    dataset = generate_data(N); # generate a data set (y,x) of length N
    theta_hat = mean(dataset[,1]); # compute sample mean of y
    mat_theta_hat[m,] = theta_hat; # store m-th sample mean
  }
  return(mat_theta_hat);
}

M = 2000; # the number of simulations (that is, the number of data sets)
print("Sampling ...")
mc_sims_100 = simulation_sample_mean(N=100, M)
print(paste("Var:", var(mc_sims_100))) # print out variance of sample means
```

This is very close to .44, as desired!

### 4. Compute skewness of $\bar{y}_N$ using Monte Carlo simulation for $N=10, 100, 1000$ (three different experiments). What do you see and explain your results.

```{r}
library(e1071) # NOTE: this library contains the skewness function, and can be installed with install.packages("e1071")
print("Additional Sampling ...")
mc_sims_10 = simulation_sample_mean(N=10, M)
mc_sims_1000 = simulation_sample_mean(N=1000, M)
print(paste("N=10:", skewness(mc_sims_10)))
print(paste("N=100:", skewness(mc_sims_100)))
print(paste("N=1000:", skewness(mc_sims_1000)))
```

At N=10 the skewness starts quite small; this makes sense, as the skewness of the chi-squared decreases as the degrees of freedom increase, while the skewness of the normal distribution remains zero. As N increases the skewness gets even smaller, as we'd expect: by the central limit theorem, the normalized sample average approaches normality as N increases; as a result, the distribution of $\bar{y}_N$ approaches a normal distribution, which has a skewness of 0.

## Q6 (Paper question)

1.  I chose the following paper; while it is from the AER, it's also about media!
2.  Wang, T. (2021). Media, Pulpit, and Populist Persuasion: Evidence from Father Coughlin. The American Economic Review, 111(9), 3064–3092. <https://www.jstor.org/stable/27086101>
3.  This paper aims to "study the impact of media manipulation by a charismatic individual" (3065) through the 1936 case of Father Charles Coughlin. A populist, fascist, and anti-Semite, Father Coughlin had a radio show from which, in the mid-1930s, he shared his opinions of the issues of the day. Comparing the strength of the radio broadcast with voting changes (cleverly addressing covariates by controlling for the strength of the radio broadcast *if there weren't topographical features,* ensuring that the main thing against which voting patterns are being measured is the strength of his broadcast itself), the author finds that a county's increased exposure to the radio program had a significant and meaningful association with FDR's vote share in that county.
4.  One of the parameters they use for the efficacy of his radio program is the "persuasion rate" (defined in more depth in DellaVigna, S., & Kaplan, E. (2007). The Fox News Effect: Media Bias and Voting. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 122(3), 1187–1234.). Since the persuasion rate is a nonlinear equation, they use the delta method to estimate its standard error.
